summary: Teach that skeletal muscles can only PULL (they contract, getting shorter and fatter) and never push. Because of this, muscles must work in opposing (antagonistic) pairs to move a bone both ways: at the elbow, the biceps contracts to bend the arm while the triceps relaxes, and the triceps contracts to straighten it while the biceps relaxes. This is felt best on the child's own upper arm. Second idea: some muscles are voluntary (arm, leg — we choose) and some are involuntary (heart, digestive muscles — automatic). The key misconception to fix is 'muscles push things back' — the partner muscle pulls the other way, and a relaxing muscle does nothing active.
misconceptions: 'Muscles push bones back into place' — muscles only PULL; the opposing muscle pulls the bone the other way.
'A single muscle moves a bone both ways' — missing that opposing pairs are needed because muscles can't push.
'When a muscle relaxes it goes limp/does nothing important' — relaxing is an active part of the pair's teamwork, letting its partner pull.
'All muscles are under our control' — missing involuntary muscles (heart, digestive muscles) that work automatically.
'The heart is not a muscle' — it is an involuntary muscle that never rests.
'Bigger muscle = the one that straightens' or other guesses — rather than reasoning from which muscle is contracting.

activities.title: Feel the pair on your own arm
steps: Place your free hand on the front of your upper arm (the biceps), then bend your elbow to raise your forearm — notice the biceps bunch up, getting shorter and harder.

Keeping your hand there, straighten your arm by pressing your palm firmly down on a table top (or pushing against a wall) — feel the biceps soften. (If you just let your forearm lower slowly on its own, gravity does most of the work and the biceps stays partly tight to control the fall, so the change is harder to feel.)

Now feel the back of your upper arm (the triceps) and press down on the table again to straighten the arm: notice that the back (triceps) tightens while the front relaxes. Straightening against a push like this is what makes the triceps work hard enough to feel.
Say out loud each time: 'Which muscle is pulling now, and which has relaxed?'
activities.insight: A contracting muscle shortens and pulls a bone; it cannot push. To move the bone back the other way, a second muscle on the opposite side must contract and pull — this is the antagonistic pair. 'Contract' and 'relax' are concrete opposites you can feel.

activities.title: Drive the elbow and discover why a pair is needed
steps: Use a model of the elbow (a driveable on-screen rig, or a cardboard hinge with an elastic band fixed on each side) where each side can act like a muscle pulling.
Make the biceps side pull only (on the band model, pull/tighten the biceps-side band to mimic the muscle contracting — shortening and pulling): watch the forearm swing up as it pulls — the arm bends.
Now try to use that SAME side to push the arm back down straight. Observe that it can only pull one way; it cannot push the bone back.
Make the triceps side pull (the other band): the arm straightens because this muscle now pulls the other way.
State the rule: one muscle pulls to bend, the other pulls to straighten, because neither can push.
activities.insight: Because a muscle can only ever pull, a single muscle can move a bone one way but is powerless to return it — so a second, opposing muscle is required. This is why muscles come in antagonistic pairs at a joint.

activities.title: Voluntary or involuntary? Sort the muscles
steps: For each muscle, ask: 'Do I choose to move it, or does it work on its own?'
Sort examples: arm muscles and leg muscles (voluntary — you decide), the heart and the muscles that squeeze food along the digestive system (involuntary — automatic).
Try the test: you can decide to bend your arm — but try to decide to stop your heart from beating. You cannot. That shows it is involuntary.
Name at least one involuntary muscle from memory (heart; digestive/gut muscles) and explain why automatic control is useful (it keeps you alive without you having to think about it).
activities.insight: Voluntary muscles are under conscious control; involuntary muscles (the heart, digestive muscles) work automatically without any decision. The heart IS a muscle — an involuntary one that never stops working, all your life.

activities.title: Consolidation check
steps: For a given movement (e.g. bending the arm), say which muscle contracts and which relaxes.
Categorise a list of muscles as voluntary or involuntary.
Match each action (bend arm / straighten arm) to the muscle that pulls to produce it.
Transfer: explain how a pair would work at another joint, or name another involuntary muscle.
activities.insight: Consolidates that muscles pull in opposing pairs and that voluntary and involuntary muscles differ, including applying the reasoning to a new joint or muscle.

checkQuestion: A muscle can only PULL, never push. So how can your arm both bend AND straighten again, if the muscle that bent it can't push it back out? And why can you decide to bend your arm, but you can't decide to stop your heart from beating?
checkAnswer: Because muscles only pull, they work in opposing PAIRS: the biceps contracts (pulls) to bend the arm while the triceps relaxes; to straighten it, the triceps contracts (pulls) the other way while the biceps relaxes. One muscle can't push the arm back, so a second muscle pulls it the other way. You can choose to bend your arm because the arm muscles are voluntary; the heart is an involuntary muscle that works automatically, so you can't decide to stop it — which keeps you alive without having to think about it.
